'''Munishvara''' or '''Munīśvara Viśvarūpa''' (born 1603) was an Indian [[mathematician]] who wrote several commentaries including one on astronomy, the ''Siddhanta Sarvabhauma'' (1646), which included descriptions of astronomical instruments such as the ''pratoda yantra''.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Ohashi, Yukio |year=1987 |title=A note on some Sanskrit manuscripts on astronomical instruments |journal=[[International Astronomical Union]] Colloquium |volume=91 |pages=191–196 |doi=10.1017/S0252921100106037 |s2cid=128504497 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Another commentary he wrote was the ''Lilavativivruti''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sinha |first=Kripa Nath |date=1985 |title=Śrîpati: An eleventh-century Indian mathematician |journal=[[Historia Mathematica]] |language=en |volume=12 |issue=1 |pages=25–44 |doi=10.1016/0315-0860(85)90066-7 |doi-access=}}</ref> Very little is known about him other than that he came from a family of astronomers including his father Ranganatha who wrote a commentary called the ''Gụ̄hārthaprakaśa/Gūḍhārthaprakāśikā,''<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nKEoAAAAYAAJ |title=The Gudhartha-Prakasaka |year=1859 |editor=Hall, F.E.}}</ref> a commentary on the ''[[Surya Siddhanta|Suryasiddhanta]]''. His grandfather Ballala had his origins in [[Dadhigrama]] in [[Vidarbha|Vidharba]] and had moved to [[Varanasi|Benares]]. Ballala had several sons who wrote commentaries on astronomy and mathematics. Munisvara's ''Siddhantasarvabhauma'' had the patronage of [[Shah Jahan]] like his paternal uncle Krishna Daivagna did. He was opposed to fellow mathematician [[Kamalakara]], whose brother also wrote a critique of Munisvara's bhangi-vibhangi method for [[planetary motion]]s. He was also opposed to the adoption of some mathematical ideas in [[spherical trigonometry]] from [[Mathematics in the medieval Islamic world|Arab scholars]].<ref>{{Citation |last=Plofker |first=Kim |chapter=Spherical Trigonometry and the Astronomy of the Medieval Kerala School |date=2002 |chapter-url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-94-015-9862-0_8 |title=History of Oriental Astronomy |volume=275 |pages=83–93 |editor-last=Ansari |editor-first=S. M. Razaullah |access-date=2022-07-18 |series=Astrophysics and Space Science Library |place=Dordrecht |publisher=Springer Netherlands |doi=10.1007/978-94-015-9862-0_8 |isbn=978-90-481-6033-4 |author-link=Kim Plofker |editor-link=S. M. Razaullah Ansari|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> An edition of his ''Siddhanta Sarvabhauma'' was published in the Princess of Wales [[Sarasvati Bhavana Granthamala]] series edited by [[Gopinath Kaviraj]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Gopinath Kaviraj|author-link=Gopinath Kaviraj|first=Munishvara|title=Siddhanta Sarvabhauma|year=1932|publisher=Sarasvati Bhavana Granthamala, No, 41.|location=Benaras}}</ref> Munisvara's book had twelve chapters in two parts. The second part had notes on astronomical instruments. He was a follower of [[Bhāskara II|Bhaskara II]].<ref>{{cite book |author=Sarma, K.V. |title=Encyclopaedia of the History of Science, Technology, and Medicine in Non-Western Cultures |publisher=Springer |year=2008 |editor=Selin, Helaine |editor-link=Helaine Selin |pages=752 |chapter=Munisvara |author-link=K. V. Sarma}}</ref>
